newsitem.title: UK: Rising Dow pushes British stocks to record close.
newsitem.headline: Rising Dow pushes British stocks to record close.

text.p: Leading British shares surged to a new record closing high on Monday, buoyed by bid speculation and by Wall Street which opened indecisively then marched ahead into record territory too.
British and German shares had hit trading records early on, but later retreated in relatively quiet trading on the ninth anniversary of the 1987 "Black Monday" crash.

While Frankfurt ended bourse trading weaker before Wall Street opened, London was inspired to surpass its morning peak. It closed at 4,073.1, up 20 points or nearly half a percent, and just a fraction off the all-time high of 4,073.2 points set late in the afternoon.
By the time the London Stock Exchange closed, the Dow Jones industrial Average was up around 25 points on the back of rallies in IBM and Texaco.
On the foreign exchange front, the dollar had slipped slightly by the end of the European day from a 33-month high of 112.86 yen set in early trading.
The weekend Japanese election result had effectively weakened the yen by doing little to alter expectations of a continuing easy money policy in Japan.
Overnight, Tokyo stocks slid sharply while government bonds surged to a record high after the poll results, which left the pro-business Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) without a clear majority.

Against the mark the dollar softened to 1.5360 from an early high of 1.5435 after news that German September M3 money supply growth, the Bundesbank's key policy indicator, had slowed. This reinforced opinions that, in the near term at least, the German central bank would not reduce interest rates.

Analysts said the Japanese election result meant it was most likely that Tokyo would go ahead with planned sales tax rises in April and modest fiscal tightening would allow the central bank to keep interest rates low.
While the "Black Monday" anniversary passed off relatively quietly on Europe's bourses, many still remained nervous that corrections in both the British and U.S. markets were overdue.

"We're seeing follow-through from Friday and the market's still fairly frothy. Dealers are saying we're going better but don't be too assured about it. There are one or two things lurking in the background," said one trader.
Traders noted that the FTSE's gains came chiefly from bid talk around media group Pearson and pharmaceuticals group Zeneca.
In early Frankfurt trading the 30-share IBIS DAX index rose 15.91 points to 2,743.47. Its previous peak was 2,739.42, hit on October 18.
Later the bourse turned down and floor trading closed weaker with dealers saying the market was consolidating following its record-breaking run.
In post bourse electronic trading German stocks revived again, boosted by Wall Street, with the Ibis Dax closing 6.11 points or almost a quarter percent higher.
French shares closed slightly easier, ignoring the fresh gains on Wall Street, on profit-taking after Friday's two-and-a-half-year closing high.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index closed down 5.01 points or 0.23 percent at 2,180.22, while the CAC-40 futures contract fell 3.5 points at 2,186.5.
CURRENCIES AT 1600 GMT
The dollar was trading at 112.70 yen and 1.5360 marks compared with Friday's London close of 112.59 yen and 1.5431 marks.
STOCKS - CLOSING PRICES
The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares ended 20.00 points higher at 4,073.1.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index finished down 5.01 at 2,180.22.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt closed down 5.79 at 2,729.03.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $381.75 compared with Friday's $380.15 London close. Silver ended up two cents $4.94.
